segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, when they first had phones around here, wasn't it like only a few phones at first? And I mean, like in the country, didn't a lot of neighbors use the same, you know, one person's one house to make their phone calls?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager

So I called him up, and the fellow just the same as told me it was none of my business. And he was going to call me and never did, so I finally could call up the state department.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: And just what, I said, what is it that there's a bank? Well, they finally told me there's a 60-some dollars. Now, after, why did they have to wait, is it over 20 years after he died? $60?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Sixty dollars?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: $60. And they're going to sell that to us. I didn't get much. So I took all this. His brother's daughter was here too for a while. Her name is Miller, and she lived right down here. So I called her up and told her what was up, and they said, what, it says a $60 over there, and they took all these papers back and forth, and sent them to her. And so if you want to take it up and see what you can do, I said, there's something crooked went on there some ways. And I guess, finally got a letter from her, and she says, well, she took it over and found out, I just said you'd have to get a, I don't know what, all the court order and all that, is to get that $60 out over there. No, thank you. She said, well, if you want us, go get us. We don't want it. We don't want to get us. I don't know what you did with it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So it looks like this banker-

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: A hundred thousand dollars went somewhere nobody knows where.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, like this banker and lawyer might have gotten into it right after he died.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: We had a little of it right in here, in town, the two or three of them already. John Donner is a fellow named Bill Earnest, kind of a feeble-minded. We had our own ranch up here, one of the best ones in the hill, never got married. And he just lived around town to the bachelor, and we figured he'd put his down well off in that one. He had a trip over the nephew here. We've got friends in here, you know, I wonder if Bill wouldn't give me some money if I write to him. He says, I can't really get around, and he wrote to him. And the home of the feeble-minded and so the night I wrote. He wrote to him, he says, he's not here. He says, you better try our phenol. Like I said, oh, oh, he tried. So I don't know, we've been talking about him. This fellow's a bank down here. He's supposed to take him down to home with feeble-minded.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: There's one of these cashiers. So I've been kind of talking around about it like this. He heard about it. He got asked me, you've been blowing off your head around here, talking about we didn't take him to home with feeble-minded. I said, did ya? He says, none of your business. I said, maybe it isn't. I'm going to find out what it is. What are you going to do? I'm going to find out where is that? I wouldn't do that if I didn't do it. I said, no, you business. I called up for a phenol. There he was over there. I've been there all the time. They took him over there. He wasn't paying nothing. So I don't know where that money went. And then he got after me. He says, after I found it, I said, well, I told him, well, he's in Orofino where you fellows took him. Well, I said, don't tell anybody. I said, too late now. He told me I was going to kick my head off. I'm going to tell everybody once in a while. That's only one of them. There's about three of them went on.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, that's what happens too, when people get old and can't take care of themselves. They're really at the mercy. They're turned over to somebody. Someone takes advantage of it.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: I was going to ask you about the Indians when you were young here. They were around town, quite a bit, weren't they? Oh, never here. They were pretty well. They were pretty darn nice.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I wasn't saying they weren't.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: They come around here. And about this time of year, they'd be up above the house. They had a whole bunch of squalls and everything. They'd taken up that canvas. They never asked for it. They just got it. And our mother used to tell about it. Some fell over in my bill for a long while. I don't got some apples or something. He'd always say he'd pay it sometimes. They'd finally come up. Had a great big fish with him and give it to her. For what I had to do with them, they wasn't bad.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know any of them personally?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Oh, there's a fellow down here. It was Charlie White. I don't know whether you've probably heard of him. He's kind of a ball player. He was a good ball player, yeah. And then he got to be quite a musician. And he was just a common everyday ball player. And then they got to be a drunkard. And then they got religious. And then somebody run over him. He was a nice, always liked him. There's another, Louis Harrison. He lived down below town here. That old Herman worked for a light company. Put in lights down there. Went down there and his wife was in bed there. And she said, I know you. How do you know me? You're out of here for it. I said, I guess you're right. I got to talk to her a little bit. And then he died. And I think she's, I don't know whether it's her or not. She's down there in a nursing home in Louis. No. Said it must be her mother or something.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, when you're saying, you're saying, Otto, that, you know, you and Herman always like to tinker and be with the, you know, work with this mechanical stuff. When do you think that started? I mean, where, well, how'd you guys have it? Why'd you have a knack for that?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: I tell you, my father's in the same family guy. He used to have a cider mill out here. And he made a darn old horsepower object. Don't think ever seem to know how to do it. Had a one horse. See, they started and raised apples. That's what's going to make you live. And well, that didn't work at all. You couldn't sell them. And so they started making cider. And making vinegar out of it. But he just turned the old cider mill and was quite a job. So he got a layout option. Run with the horsepower. Just, and then he was quite pretty good that way. I think we inherited that. Same with my not hearing anything. I think I inherited that too.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So when you first started tinkering, was it just watching your father do his work?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Well, we had a binder about the first thing. And we had to keep that thing going. By the guy that was about the first machine we worked on. And it must have been pretty, kind of a number of years ago. Was when he bought it with Herman, I went downtown with him. Herman, he couldn't walk. And they laid him on that back from the binder so he could ride. So I don't know what just went that far. But that is our job. Always gets the binder going. I got to work with the threshing outfit. Wasn't there no time I got it. Had to run the separator. It's just kind of a knife on a machinery and electric stuff.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did your father ever say, ever tell you why he picked this place to homestead?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Well, I tell you, if you read that history, I might tell about as much as anything.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I don't think Herman said why, you know, why he, I mean, I know he.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Well, they all want to get out of Austria there. And I think the war more than anything else. But when we went to school, one of the things is, why is the United States so much better than other countries? Because there's no military training. And no, what else was it? No income tax. Now we got them both. And that is one that got out. I don't know how he got out. But I know I think Eichner, I think he sneaked out somewhere out the back door. And a lot of them did. And my uncle come in and had a boy, Joe Schupfer. Well, he'd be Charlie Nova's, the same relation to him who was the me. No, it wasn't me. He was my other brother. And he come over with them. And they got somebody to settle over there. They put in their toilet houses a piece over trying to find him. They figured he ought to be in Austria somewhere. In fact, the First World War, they couldn't find him nowhere. But he was over here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So they wanted to leave because they didn't like the, they didn't like the having to go in the military and the state, the power of the state.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: And the income tax. Now we got the biggest income tax of anybody, I guess. Got the biggest throwing away money there ever was.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, how did you feel about the war? I imagine, I know a lot of Swedish guys didn't want to go in that First World War.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: I didn't see we had no business in it.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, I mean, if they had, you know, I mean, like some guy, all these guys that got drafted, they had to go in there.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But they never did draft you. You didn't get drafted then.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Put in there. My number was coming up just about another month or two after I, when I come back from Sunday side, they come back to fill out the application or something. But I was led out to begin with because running this telephone outfit, there's nobody else could run it. So that they put in the class down the line always.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did many of the German kids from around Cameron have to go?

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: Oh, heck, just as many as the English ones. Oh, they'll start another one. I look one of the girls before this wage deal goes quits out by these fellows and say, you're going to work for less money. Well, they'll fight before they work.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you know, the army's got pretty good pay now compared to what it used to be.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: They, yes, they have.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The volunteer army, the pay is, in fact, I understand.

segments.speaker: Otto Schupfer
segments.words: That none of the none of our bunch, let's see, what is his slogan? If he gets elected, he's had to be elected. He said nobody gets elected. Nobody's go over. Yeah, I think he said he kept us out of war. I kept us out of war. That is it. And it was in about two weeks until he was in. Well, the next one was Roosevelt. No American boys will ever go overseas. Well, he wasn't anymore. They said him over the fact that he could settle over there. Because the United States that over attend their own business and clean up some of the outfit back they've got here. Like these guys who don't want to work unless they get a year later in the day.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, well, that's one of the things...
